title: Repair Negotiations Training
summary: Comprehensive training on repair negotiations from both buyer and listing agent perspectives. Covers the three buckets of negotiation items (safety/health, big ticket, cosmetic), scripting for aggressive but ethical negotiations, upfront disclosure strategies for listing agents, and handling common objections. Includes specific tactics for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, roofing, meth, radon, and structural issues.

broker_guidance.guidance: Categorize requests into three buckets: (1) Safety/Health, (2) Big Ticket Items, (3) Cosmetic/Visible. Lead with safety/health items and use strong language: 'These are significant safety concerns that could cause the buyer to withdraw.'
broker_guidance.client_language: These are significant safety and health concerns to the degree that the buyer would back out if not addressed.

broker_guidance.guidance: Electrical items are 'no brainers' for safety bucket. Includes double-tapped wires, ungrounded outlets, old panels with known failure rates, aluminum wiring. Get inspector to document known failure rates for older panels.
broker_guidance.client_language: This is a safety issue. We want this panel replaced.

broker_guidance.guidance: Actively leaking plumbing = safety/health (mold/structural). Galvanized water lines can be negotiated even if working - disclose to next buyer argument works. Sewer mainline issues are 'pretty easy negotiation' when scoped.
broker_guidance.client_language: These plumbing issues create mold problems and potential structural damage.

broker_guidance.guidance: Best negotiated UPFRONT before inspection by asking ages during showing. If old, get price reduction or warranty at offer stage. If seller misrepresents age (says 5 years, turns out 15), you have clear runway to demand credit.
broker_guidance.client_language: We offered under the assumption the furnace was 5 years old. Turns out it's 15. We did not anticipate that.

broker_guidance.scenario: Meth test results below state limit
broker_guidance.guidance: State limit is 1.0 (divided number). If aggregate exceeds 1.0 but divided is below 1.0 = 'trace amount.' Focus on HVAC/furnace cleanse since that's where traces congregate. Below 0.5 = very difficult to get concessions. Buyers are less scared of low traces now.
broker_guidance.client_language: The aggregate score exceeds 1.0 which indicates contamination. The hot spots are in the HVAC system where traces have congregated.

broker_guidance.guidance: Disclose ages of roof, HVAC, furnace, water heater in AGENT REMARKS (not public). When buyer later requests repairs, point out it was disclosed upfront. Use: 'You're buying a 1950s home. Some stuff will be new, some won't. We didn't advertise this as brand new.' Offer 2-year home warranty as compromise.
broker_guidance.client_language: That was known upfront - it was right there in the listing details. We put the specific year so this would be avoided.

broker_guidance.scenario: Buyer agent worried about pushing too hard
broker_guidance.guidance: Act as if this is YOUR purchase or your sibling's. Don't hold back to avoid losing the deal. Buyers appreciate aggressive representation. Get buyer permission to be aggressive: 'Can I give the indication these are concerning enough that you may back out?'
broker_guidance.client_language: I'm going to fight for everything on this list. The next buyer is going to reasonably request these things too.

broker_guidance.guidance: Credits going directly to contractors do NOT count as seller contribution to buyer. Can have 20% of home value go to contractors without hitting contribution limits. Name contractor on settlement statement. Doesn't show on buyer's settlement statement, so doesn't influence underwriting.
broker_guidance.client_language: We'll have the seller credit $18,000 directly to the roofing contractor at closing. This won't affect your loan.

broker_guidance.guidance: Never succeed: cracks in concrete (100% visible at walkthrough), carpet condition (visible), negative slope (common on older homes), trees unless power line safety issue. Tell buyers upfront these won't work.
broker_guidance.client_language: The driveway condition was visible when you walked through. It's not fair to come back now and ask for help with something you already saw.

broker_guidance.scenario: Handling inspection report with listing agent
broker_guidance.guidance: Listing agent is legally required to forward inspection report to seller (fiduciary duty). What agent knows, principal knows. If seller counters and removes some repairs, the lender may see unfixed items and stipulate they be fixed. Better to let addendum lapse and verbally agree, then resubmit only agreed items.
broker_guidance.client_language: You're required to provide this inspection report to your seller. It's your fiduciary responsibility under agency law.

steps: Categorize inspection findings into: Safety/Health, Big Ticket Items, Cosmetic
Lead with safety/health items using strong withdrawal language
Get buyer permission to be aggressive in negotiations
For old systems, try to negotiate upfront at offer stage by asking ages during showing
If seller misrepresents system ages, use that as leverage post-inspection
For contractor credits, name contractor on settlement statement (doesn't count as contribution)
Always recommend all inspections upfront (sewer scope, meth, radon) to limit liability
Set due diligence deadline with buffer time - don't negotiate same day as deadline
For listing agents: disclose system ages in agent remarks to preempt repair requests
If buyer submits too many repairs and seller will only do some, let addendum lapse and verbally negotiate

objections.objection: Seller says they'll just buy a home warranty
objections.response: That's not enough for old systems. Push for 2-year warranty or credit. If they refuse, hammer price upfront knowing these items are old.

objections.objection: Seller says buyer already saw the condition before offer
objections.response: For visible items (carpet, cracks), that's correct - don't negotiate. For hidden issues (electrical, plumbing), those weren't visible and are fair game.

objections.objection: Listing agent won't forward inspection report to seller
objections.response: They are legally required to. It's fiduciary duty. What the agent knows, the principal must know. Not forwarding opens them to liability.

objections.objection: Seller calls bluff on buyer backing out
objections.response: Keep pushing until due diligence deadline. Time is on your side. Many sellers fold rather than risk starting over.

objections.objection: Multiple offer situation - can't negotiate upfront
objections.response: Don't ask for ages upfront in multiple offer situations. Get under contract first, then address after inspection.
